title: Meetings & reporting (hōrensō)
intro:
One of the first workplace concepts you will hear about is {報連相[ほうれんそう]} (hōrensō), a pun on the word for spinach. It stands for three habits that Japanese managers value highly:

- {報告[ほうこく]} (report): tell your boss about progress and results, without waiting to be asked. Report bad news, such as delays and mistakes, early.
- {連絡[れんらく]} (inform): share facts, such as schedule changes and absences, with everyone affected.
- {相談[そうだん]} (consult): ask for advice before making a decision or when you are stuck, rather than deciding alone.

When reporting, start with the conclusion ({結論[けつろん]から申[もう]しますと}), then the reason, then what you propose.

Meetings range from formal {会議[かいぎ]} to smaller working sessions ({打[う]ち合[あ]わせ}). In many Japanese organizations, important decisions are prepared before the meeting through informal consultation with key people ({根回[ねまわ]し}), so the meeting itself often confirms what was already discussed. If you want to propose something, talk to the right people beforehand.

Junior members are often asked to take minutes ({議事録[ぎじろく]}). When you disagree, soften it: acknowledge the other view first ({おっしゃることはよくわかります}), then give yours ({ただ、〜}). A phrase you will hear from clients is {持[も]ち帰[かえ]って検討[けんとう]いたします} (we'll take this back and consider it), which means no decision today. Written approval flows ({稟議[りんぎ]}) are also common for spending and new projects.

phrases.jp: 今[いま]、少[すこ]しお時間[じかん]よろしいでしょうか。
phrases.en: Do you have a moment now?

phrases.jp: A社[しゃ]の件[けん]で、ご報告[ほうこく]があります。
phrases.en: I have a report about Company A.

phrases.jp: 結論[けつろん]から申[もう]しますと、
予定[よてい]より2日[ふつか]ほど遅[おく]れています。
phrases.en: We're about two days behind schedule.

phrases.jp: ご相談[そうだん]したいことがあるのですが。
phrases.en: There's something I'd like to consult you about.

phrases.jp: どのように進[すす]めればよろしいでしょうか。
明日[あした]の会議[かいぎ]は、14時[じゅうよじ]からに変更[へんこう]になりました。
phrases.en: Tomorrow's meeting has been changed to start at 2 p.m.

phrases.jp: 念[ねん]のため、皆[みな]さんにも共有[きょうゆう]しておきます。
phrases.en: Just in case, I'll share this with everyone too.

phrases.jp: 一[ひと]つ、よろしいでしょうか。
おっしゃることはよくわかります。ただ、
phrases.en: I understand what you're saying. However, ...

phrases.jp: 私[わたし]の理解[りかい]が正[ただ]しいか、確認[かくにん]させてください。
phrases.en: Let me check whether I've understood correctly.

phrases.jp: その件[けん]は持[も]ち帰[かえ]って検討[けんとう]いたします。
phrases.en: We'll take that back and consider it.

phrases.jp: では、本日[ほんじつ]の決定[けってい]事項[じこう]を確認[かくにん]します。
議事録[ぎじろく]は私[わたし]が作成[さくせい]して、後[のち]ほどお送[おく]りします。
phrases.en: I'll write the minutes and send them later.

phrases.jp: 私[わたし]のミスです。申[もう]し訳[わけ]ありません。すぐに対応[たいおう]します。
phrases.en: It was my mistake. I'm sorry. I'll deal with it right away.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.jp: 課長[かちょう]、今[いま]、少[すこ]しお時間[じかん]よろしいでしょうか。
dialogue.en: Section manager, do you have a moment now?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.jp: 新[しん]システムの件[けん]でご報告[ほうこく]です。結論[けつろん]から申[もう]しますと、テストが予定[よてい]より3日[みっか]ほど遅[おく]れています。
dialogue.en: It's a report on the new system. To start with the conclusion, testing is about three days behind schedule.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.jp: そうか。原因[げんいん]は？

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.jp: 先方[せんぽう]からのデータの提供[ていきょう]が遅[おく]れたためです。
dialogue.en: The client was late providing the data.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.jp: リリース日[び]には間[ま]に合[あ]いそう？
dialogue.en: Will we make the release date?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.jp: 週末[しゅうまつ]までにデータが届[とど]けば、間[ま]に合[あ]います。そこでご相談[そうだん]なのですが、先方[せんぽう]に課長[かちょう]からも一言[ひとこと]お願[ねが]いできないでしょうか。
dialogue.en: If the data arrives by the weekend, we will. So I'd like to ask: could you also have a word with the client?

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.jp: わかった。今日中[きょうじゅう]に連絡[れんらく]しておく。早[はや]めに言[い]ってくれて助[たす]かったよ。
dialogue.en: OK. I'll contact them today. Thanks for telling me early.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.jp: ありがとうございます。進捗[しんちょく]はまた明日[あした]ご報告[ほうこく]いたします。
dialogue.en: Thank you. I'll report on progress again tomorrow.

tips: Bad news first and early. A delay reported on day one is a small problem; the same delay reported on the deadline is a big one.
Before an important meeting, talk privately with key people about your idea. Surprising people in the meeting itself rarely works well.
Volunteer to take minutes when you are new. It is a great way to learn names, jargon and how decisions are made.
Clients and partners are often called {先方[せんぽう]} (the other party) internally.
If you are confused in a meeting, write down your questions and ask your senior colleague afterward.
